## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Nanduttarātherīgāthā* (Thig 5.5) is a short poem preserved in the *Therīgāthā* (numbered as text xlii in older arrangements, containing verses 87–91) that records the verses of the elder nun Nanduttarā [Jennings 1948; Horner 1930; Blackstone 2000]. Born into a brahmin family, Nanduttarā initially engaged in traditional religious practices, worshipping fire, the moon, the sun, and gods, and undertaking ritual bathings at river-fords [Horner 1930; Blackstone 2000]. She subsequently became a Jain mendicant, engaging in severe austerities such as sleeping on the bare ground, shaving half of her head, and fasting until evening [Wijayaratna 1990; Horner 1930]. Renowned as a sharp intellect, orator, and formidable public debater, she is associated in commentarial accounts with planting a rose-apple branch as an open debate challenge before being converted to Buddhism through an encounter with the venerable Mahā-Moggallāna [Horner 1930; Collett 2009].
In her verses, Nanduttarā looks back critically upon her pre-Buddhist wandering and ascetic practices, condemning them as fruitless ceremonies that merely amounted to "ministering to the body" spurred by sense desires (verse 89) [Blackstone 2000; Horner 1930]. She declares that liberation was ultimately attained not through external mortifications, but through "seeing the body as it really was" within the Buddhist teaching (verse 90) [Blackstone 2000].
